notes: Applies to all fifteen checkpoints: 128/256-bit keys, 8/12/20 rounds. RFC 8439 specifies the 20-round, 256-bit IETF variant; the common round construction is also specified by djb-chacha-2008 sections 2.2 and 3.2. This is not a claim of IETF nonce-layout compliance. All four additions, XORs, rotations, and output words are one record. Source line wrapping normalized.

text: The first four words (0-3) are constants: 0x61707865, 0x3320646e, 0x79622d32, 0x6b206574.
notes: 256-bit checkpoints only, across 8/12/20 rounds. RFC supplies all four values; djb-chacha-2008 section 3.2 retains Salsa20 constants without spelling them out. The reduced-round adoption is established by the original RTL and bench; no RFC requirement for 8/12 rounds is claimed.

text: With keylen=0, state words 0-3 are 0x61707865, 0x3120646e, 0x79622d36, 0x6b206574, respectively. These four words encode the bytes of "expand 16-byte k" in little-endian order.
notes: 128-bit checkpoints only, across 8/12/20 rounds. All four TAU words are treated together. Neither permitted document spells out these four values: the paper section 3.2 refers to Salsa20 constants, and RFC 8439 excludes 128-bit expansion. Source is therefore the original RTL and checker.

text: The next eight words (4-11) are taken from the 256-bit key by reading the bytes in little-endian order, in 4-byte chunks.
notes: 256-bit checkpoints only, across 8/12/20 rounds. RFC explicitly states byte interpretation; paper section 3.2 states key ordering. Applying it to reduced-round configurations is corroborated by RTL and bench. All eight key words are included.

text: With keylen=0, the four byte-reversed words from key[255:128] initialize state words 4-7 and repeat in words 8-11. key[127:0] does not supply a second independent group of key words in this mode.
notes: 128-bit checkpoints only, across 8/12/20 rounds. All eight state positions are specified together. The permitted paper does not explicitly state this repetition rule; RFC 8439 places 128-bit keys outside its defined configuration.

text: The initial state has sixteen 32-bit words arranged in four rows of four words. Reading rows from top to bottom and words from left to right, positions 0-3 contain constants, positions 4-7 and 8-11 contain the eight key words, and positions 12-15 contain the two counter words followed by the two nonce words.
notes: Citation: Daniel J. Bernstein, ChaCha, a variant of Salsa20 (2008-01-28), section 3.2, PDF page 5. Technical facts restated by the curator; no paper sentences reproduced. All sixteen state words are mapped together for all fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints. The paper establishes matrix roles and ordering; RFC 8439 section 2.3, printed page 8, confirms the original 64-bit counter and nonce widths, and the original RTL confirms their two-word placement. The 128-bit key repetition, precise constants, and boundary byte conversion remain separately identified RTL inferences or RFC statements.

text: An accepted init loads ctr[31:0] into the low counter half and ctr[63:32] into the high half. Initial state words 12 and 13 receive those halves respectively, without l2b conversion. The supplied bench ties the complete ctr input to zero for every comparison.
notes: All fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints use counter zero. Both halves are included uniformly; nonzero counter loading and inter-half ordering cannot be independently distinguished by these vectors. Paper section 3.2 gives counter-before-nonce order; RFC 8439 section 2.3 page 8 explicitly acknowledges the original 64-bit counter and nonce.

text: State words 14 and 15 receive l2b(iv[63:32]) and l2b(iv[31:0]), respectively, supplying the two words of the 64-bit IV. Both words are retained in initial-state addition at the end of the block.
notes: All fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints; nonzero IVs occur in checkpoints 9-15. Paper section 3.2 gives counter-before-nonce ordering; RFC 8439 section 2.3 page 8 acknowledges the original 64-bit nonce. Exact two-word byte mapping is established here by the RTL and checker, not by the paper text.

text:
QUARTERROUND(0, 4, 8, 12)
QUARTERROUND(1, 5, 9, 13)
QUARTERROUND(2, 6, 10, 14)
QUARTERROUND(3, 7, 11, 15)
notes: Applies to all fifteen checkpoints: 128/256-bit keys, 8/12/20 rounds. RFC 8439 specifies the 20-round, 256-bit IETF variant; the common round construction is also specified by djb-chacha-2008 sections 2.2 and 3.2. This is not a claim of IETF nonce-layout compliance. These are the four column groups; all sixteen positions and their returns are included. RFC labels groups 1-4 as the column round; paper section 3.2 lists the same groups.

text:
QUARTERROUND(0, 5, 10, 15)
QUARTERROUND(1, 6, 11, 12)
QUARTERROUND(2, 7, 8, 13)
QUARTERROUND(3, 4, 9, 14)
notes: Applies to all fifteen checkpoints: 128/256-bit keys, 8/12/20 rounds. RFC 8439 specifies the 20-round, 256-bit IETF variant; the common round construction is also specified by djb-chacha-2008 sections 2.2 and 3.2. This is not a claim of IETF nonce-layout compliance. These are the four diagonal groups, following each column round; all sixteen positions and their returns are included. Paper section 3.2 lists the same groups.

text: ChaCha8 performs 8 rounds, starting with a column round and then alternating column and diagonal rounds. A double round consists of one column round followed by one diagonal round, so the transformation comprises 4 double rounds.
notes: Citation: Daniel J. Bernstein, ChaCha, a variant of Salsa20 (2008-01-28), Abstract, PDF page 1, and section 3.2, PDF page 5. Technical facts restated by the curator; no paper sentences reproduced. Applies to the listed 8-round checkpoints for both key sizes. The paper defines the named round counts; its abstract describes 256-bit keys, while use with 128-bit expansion is established by the RTL and bench. RFC 8439 does not define the 8-round variant.

text: ChaCha12 performs 12 rounds, starting with a column round and then alternating column and diagonal rounds. A double round consists of one column round followed by one diagonal round, so the transformation comprises 6 double rounds.
notes: Citation: Daniel J. Bernstein, ChaCha, a variant of Salsa20 (2008-01-28), Abstract, PDF page 1, and section 3.2, PDF page 5. Technical facts restated by the curator; no paper sentences reproduced. Applies to the listed 12-round checkpoints for both key sizes. The paper defines the named round counts; its abstract describes 256-bit keys, while use with 128-bit expansion is established by the RTL and bench. RFC 8439 does not define the 12-round variant.

text: ChaCha20 performs 20 rounds, starting with a column round and then alternating column and diagonal rounds. A double round consists of one column round followed by one diagonal round, so the transformation comprises 10 double rounds.
notes: Citation: Daniel J. Bernstein, ChaCha, a variant of Salsa20 (2008-01-28), Abstract, PDF page 1, and section 3.2, PDF page 5. Technical facts restated by the curator; no paper sentences reproduced. Applies to the listed 20-round checkpoints for both key sizes. The paper defines the named round counts; its abstract describes 256-bit keys, while use with 128-bit expansion is established by the RTL and bench. RFC 8439 section 2.3 also specifies 20 rounds for its 256-bit IETF configuration.

text:
At the end of 20 rounds (or 10 iterations of the above list), we add the original input words to the output words, and serialize the result by sequencing the words one-by-one in little-endian order.

Note: "addition" in the above paragraph is done modulo 2^32.
notes: Applies to all fifteen checkpoints: 128/256-bit keys, 8/12/20 rounds. RFC 8439 specifies the 20-round, 256-bit IETF variant; the common round construction is also specified by djb-chacha-2008 sections 2.2 and 3.2. This is not a claim of IETF nonce-layout compliance. Quoted text is the RFC 20-round statement. Paper section 3.2 supplies final addition after r rounds; its 8/12-round application is thus separately grounded. This record covers all sixteen corresponding sums modulo 2^32, not a 20-round requirement for every checkpoint.

text: At the end of 20 rounds (or 10 iterations of the above list), we add the original input words to the output words, and serialize the result by sequencing the words one-by-one in little-endian order.
notes: All fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints use the same serialization. The quoted RFC wording explicitly applies at 20 rounds. Paper section 3.2 gives output word ordering but leaves the byte convention implicit in Salsa20; extending the RFC byte convention to the remaining configurations is corroborated by the original RTL and checker, recorded separately in interface.l2b. No claim that the paper explicitly defines byte conversion is made.

text: The core forms data_out_new by XORing the entire 512-bit data_in with the serialized 16-word block. The bench holds data_in at zero, so every expected comparison checks the resulting keystream block.
notes: All fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints. RFC 8439 section 2.4 describes stream XOR for its IETF variant. Nonzero data_in, partial blocks, and encryption/decryption sequences are not exercised; these checks do not independently establish general XOR behavior.

text: This core implements ChaCha with support for 128 and 256 bit keys. The number of rounds can be set from two to 32 rounds in steps of two.
notes: Repository claim only. The fifteen checkpoints exercise both key sizes and only 8/12/20 rounds. Other round values, including the claimed 32-round endpoint on a five-bit port, are not validated here. NUM_ROUNDS is unused in the examined RTL; the bench drives rounds.

text: The core has four separate quarterround modules, which means that one round takes one cycle.
notes: Applies as a repository architectural claim to the 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round configurations. All four instances are mapped uniformly. The bench waits for data_out_valid without comparing cycle counts, so no checkpoint verifies this exact timing claim; wrapper latency is outside scope.

text: Each comparison resets the core, sets key, keylen, iv, and rounds, pulses init for one clock period, deasserts init, then waits for a rising data_out_valid before comparing all 512 output bits. The input parameters remain stable during that block.
notes: All fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints. This is the supplied bench protocol, not a published-document interface requirement. Requests while processing and init from CTRL_DONE are not exercised by the compared sequences.

text: In CTRL_DONE, init starts a fresh block with ctr loaded; otherwise next starts another block after incrementing the internal counter. An init request takes precedence when both are asserted. The bench leaves next low and resets before each compared block.
notes: Observed RTL behavior for both key sizes and the 8/12/20-round settings; no checkpoint exercises next, simultaneous requests, or continuation. This record makes no claim that the published documents define these port semantics.

text: The RTL sets ready on reset and final output capture, and clears it when starting an accepted request. The bench connects ready but waits on data_out_valid and compares data_out; ready does not gate its comparisons.
notes: Observed across the supported 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round configurations. No checkpoint independently checks ready, its transitions, or latency. Source is original RTL and bench, not RFC or paper.

text: Reset clears data_out_valid. Finalization captures data_out and asserts data_out_valid on the same rising clock edge. The bench resumes on the rising edge of this valid signal and compares the complete block. In CTRL_DONE a new accepted init or next clears the valid signal.
notes: All fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints depend on the first post-reset valid event and output availability. They do not independently check exact latency, duration of valid, or its clearing by a continuation request. Port behavior is inferred from original RTL and bench.

text: keylen=0 selects the 128-bit expansion and keylen=1 selects the 256-bit expansion. The bench sets keylen with key and iv before init and leaves it stable through output capture.
notes: All fifteen checkpoints: ten 128-bit and five 256-bit, with 8/12/20 rounds. Numeric port encodings are established by the RTL and checker. Changing keylen during a block is not tested.

text: The bench drives rounds to 8, 12, or 20 and keeps it stable. The core alternates column and diagonal rounds and compares the double-round counter against rounds[4:1]-1 after each diagonal round, executing 4, 6, or 10 pairs respectively.
notes: All fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints. This describes port encoding and implementation sequencing; named round counts come from the paper. NUM_ROUNDS is not read by the logic. Odd values, other even values, and input changes while processing are not checked.

text: On an accepted next request, the low 32-bit counter half increases by one. The high 32-bit half increases by one when the previous low half is 0xffffffff and otherwise retains its value. Both halves are 32-bit registers. An accepted init loads both halves from ctr.
notes: Observed RTL behavior for both key sizes and 8/12/20 rounds; no checkpoint exercises increment, carry, or wrap because ctr is zero and next stays low. Both counter halves are treated together. Initial zero-counter loading is separately associated with all checkpoints in state.counter.

text: l2b maps a 32-bit word to {op[7:0], op[15:8], op[23:16], op[31:24]}. The core applies it uniformly to each supplied key word, both IV words, and all sixteen final summed words. Output words 0 through 15 occupy successive 32-bit slices from data_out[511:480] through data_out[31:0]. Counter halves enter the state numerically without this conversion.
notes: All fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints. Exact packed-vector boundary behavior is inferred from original RTL and bench. RFC 8439 states the little-endian word convention for its IETF configuration; the paper leaves byte interpretation implicit in Salsa20. All peer words are treated uniformly.

text: Before every known-answer comparison the bench asserts reset_n low for a clock period, releases it on a falling clock edge, and waits another clock period before supplying the request. The RTL uses a synchronous active-low reset, returns to CTRL_IDLE, clears the state and both counter halves, and clears data_out_valid.
notes: All fifteen 128/256-bit, 8/12/20-round checkpoints depend on reaching the initial request sequence. Individual reset register values and reset during an active block are not independently compared. Source is original RTL and bench.
